tasks.short: Prepare the check with the candidate's training record, conduct the proficiency check, debrief the candidate, decide and complete the examiner report, send it to the authority and operator, and sign the licence entry.

steps.what: Airline pilot prepares the proficiency check scenario and reads the candidate's training record
Airline pilot evaluates other pilots or license applicants for proficiency in the simulator or aircraft
Airline pilot decides the result of the proficiency check
Airline pilot completes the examiner report: on paper today; after the change in the training system with candidate and aircraft data filled in, where the operator's copy is saved
Airline pilot checks the final examiner report: the result and remarks match the check flown and the debrief, and candidate, licence and aircraft are right
Airline pilot submits the checked examiner report to the authority: by post or e-mail today; one submission from the form after the change
Airline pilot signs the licence entry

tasks.design: The candidate's training history and earlier checks show in the training system ({LMS}), so the examiner prepares without asking for paper files. The examiner report is an electronic form in the authority's template in the training system with candidate and aircraft data filled in; the operator's copy is saved there. The examiner writes the result and remarks, checks the report and submits it to the authority. Conducting the check, debriefing, deciding and signing the licence stay with the examiner; no software grades the candidate.
tasks.previous_blocker: Training files were paper and examiner reports were filled by hand and posted or e-mailed.
tasks.enabler_now: Training systems hold training records; examiner forms can be completed electronically.
tasks.still_hard: A fail decision has to be fair and well explained.
tasks.human_edge: Telling a nervous candidate's error apart from a real gap in skill.

reach.learn: Whether reports arrive the same day.

evidence.claim: Training systems can hold training records and electronic examiner forms.
AI that evaluates learning outcomes in vocational training is high-risk under Annex III point 3; here no software grades the candidate.

assumptions: Boundary: from the check booking to the licence signed; retraining is outside.
Input contract: training records from the operator; report templates from the authority; fallback is paper.

Conducting, deciding, signing and the check keep their full time. s5 keeps 75 because only candidate and aircraft data fill in and the examiner writes the result and remarks; s6 keeps 20 for the submission; s1 keeps 70 because records show in the training system instead of being asked for. Checking the filled-in data is inside s5c, so there is no new work.
The authority accepts electronic examiner reports.
research_questions: Do reports reach the authority sooner?

incremental.description: No new work: checking the filled-in candidate data is part of the check in s5c.

approvals.approved_version: The examiner report with result and remarks exactly as checked and signed by the examiner in s5c, submitted once to the authority for this candidate's licence; any change needs a new check and signature.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: older records are not in the training system (s1 keeps 85) and the authority takes electronic reports for only some licences (s6 keeps 60) (5.5); high: records and submission are electronic as designed (9.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Plan flight test activities and test points, build the test schedule, record results on test cards in flight, write the flight evaluation report, send it to engineering, and discuss findings.

steps.what: Airline pilot plans and formulates flight activities and test points
Airline pilot builds the test schedule with aircraft and crew availability
Airline pilot records results on test cards in flight: on paper today; on tablet cards after the change, where recorded flight data fill the values and the pilot writes ratings and comments
Airline pilot prepares the flight evaluation report

loop.input: The completed test cards, the recorded flight data and the pilot's notes.
loop.output: A draft flight evaluation report per test point.
loop.check: Code checks that every number in the text matches the recorded data and every test point has a result; the pilot reads each finding against the cards and data, checks that the conclusion follows from the result and its limits, and rewrites any finding that does not.
loop.stop: Stops when the checks pass and the pilot approves, or after two failed redrafts the pilot writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: Findings need a pilot's explanation in prose; a template can only list the numbers.

steps.what: Airline pilot checks the final evaluation report: each conclusion matches the test results, and limits and unexpected behaviour are stated
Airline pilot sends the checked evaluation report to engineering
Airline pilot discusses the findings with engineers

tasks.design: Test cards start from templates per test type in the document space ({DOCS}). A planning board joins aircraft slots with crew availability from the crew system ({OPS_SYSTEM}). In flight, results go on tablet test cards linked to recorded flight data. A bounded step drafts the result tables and a first text of the evaluation report from the cards and data; code checks every number against the data, and the pilot reads each finding against the cards and rewrites the assessment. The pilot checks the final report and sends it to engineering. Planning test points and discussing findings stay with the pilot.
tasks.previous_blocker: Test cards were built by hand, results written on paper and reports typed from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Tablet test cards link to flight data; language models draft reports from structured results.
tasks.still_hard: Unexpected aircraft behaviour needs the pilot's own words.
tasks.human_edge: Describing how the aircraft felt in a way engineers can act on.
tasks.altitude: The pilot edits reports instead of typing them.

reach.learn: Whether reports arrive sooner after flights.

evidence.claim: Language models can draft reports from structured test results with numbers checked against the source data.
Aviation products sit in AI Act Annex I, so AI rules come through EASA; this drafting step does not touch aircraft systems.

assumptions: Boundary: from the test request to findings agreed; design changes are outside.
Input contract: test requests from engineering; flight data from the aircraft recorder; fallback is paper cards and typing.

Discussing findings and the check keep their full time. s1 keeps 80 because templates give the card layout and standard items while the pilot plans the test points; s2 keeps 50; s3 keeps 60 because recorded data replace values read off instruments while ratings and comments are still written; s4 keeps 65 because tables and results fill from the cards and the pilot writes the assessment; s5 keeps 20 for the send.
Test data stay inside the operator's systems.
research_questions: How much of the drafted report does the pilot change?

already_counted.description: Airline pilot edits and approves the drafted report.

incremental.description: Airline pilot keeps test card templates current.

approvals.approved_version: The evaluation report exactly as checked by the pilot in s4c, sent once to the requesting engineering team; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most tests are one-off with new card types, so templates and drafts help little and s1 keeps 90, s4 keeps 85 (25.1); high: repeat test types with standard cards as designed (32.4).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The airline pilot keeps judging proficiency, planning test points and explaining findings; paper files, hand-filled forms and typed reports shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A pilot who spends saved time on better checks and tests.

job.title: Airline Pilots, Copilots, and Flight Engineers
